finding: §2 asserts an equivalence the release does not buy, and it is the one equivalence that costs the loop its safety. It says an operator setting `blocking` "is choosing to gate on the audited agent's own judgement, which is the same standing decision as `--skip-gate`". `--skip-gate` is fenced: under TP_UNATTENDED=1 it exits 2 and the unit must `tp escalate` (internal/cli/unattended.go:29-38; unattended_fence_test.go:33). `audit_converge_on` would not be. The fence's only workflow-write entry point is fenceWorkflowWrite(field string, requested float64) (unattended.go:56-76), which is numeric by signature and refuses only FencedCapField/FencedCommandField; a string workflow field never reaches it. So under `tp run` a unit that cannot converge could write `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and end its own audit phase on its own authority -- the exact substitution the fence exists to prevent, arriving as a field the release itself calls equivalent to a fenced decision. It is also the first such field: `review_converge_on`'s weaker value IS its default, so no unit can weaken review convergence by writing it; `audit_converge_on` is the first workflow field whose non-default value relaxes a gate. The spec decides the default, the vocabulary and the fail-closed rule, and never decides who may set it.
suggestion: Decide it in §2 in one sentence and test it. Either the field joins §5.1's fence -- name its escalation decision, add it to the fenced set, and add a test that `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` exits 2 under TP_UNATTENDED=1 -- or state that it is deliberately unfenced and why the `--skip-gate` analogy does not carry, and delete that sentence from §2. Asserting the analogy while leaving the fence unspecified is the one combination that reads as decided and is not.

finding: §2 reinstates, word for word, a precedence sentence a SHIPPED release already measured false and withdrew. §2: 'resolved through the same precedence every workflow field uses (CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in)'. spec/0.35.0.md §7 lines 569-578 says the opposite and records why: 'the precedence for workflow fields is **task override > project config > built-in**: tp exposes no CLI flag and reads no `TP_<FIELD>` environment variable for any of them, so the two upper layers named elsewhere in tp's documentation are absent here rather than merely unused' -- followed by 'An earlier draft of this section wrote the precedence as `CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in`. The audit's spec-coverage role reported, across two rounds, that the top two layers could not be verified because nothing implements them -- a claim no test can settle either way. The text now states what resolves.' Verified against the code rather than the sibling spec: engine/configresolve.go:233-269 ResolveWorkflowLayers merges exactly two layers over the built-in default (pickString([]*string{taskOverride.X, project.X}, def.X)) for every field including ReviewConvergeOn:261; and a repo-wide search for `TP_REVIEW_CONVERGE_ON|review-converge-on` returns 0 matches, so the twin this section names has neither of the two layers it claims. This is not the round-1 'no precedence is documented' finding: that one was repaired by ADDING a precedence, and the precedence added is the one v0.35.0's audit spent two rounds removing. Its cost is concrete: §5 test 1 asks for resolution 'through the full precedence chain', which is unwritable -- no fixture can exercise a CLI or env layer that no code reads -- so the release's only precedence test either asserts three layers while the spec claims five, or is abandoned.
suggestion: Replace the parenthesis with the form spec/0.35.0.md §7 shipped: 'task override > project config > built-in'. Then restate test 1 over those three layers, and add the surface sentence §7 also carries -- '`tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new field on the same terms as every existing workflow field' -- which is what v0.31.1 exists to have missed for `review_converge_on`.

finding: "Prospective only. The reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward" names no observable that separates a round recorded before this release from one recorded after, so tests 5 and 8 cannot be written. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json: every one of the nine recorded audit rounds already carries a spec_hash (1acd1448, 1acd1448, 7fcdbba3, 853f2c5b, 7f5bad9a, 2157b252, dc61f3d9, dc61f3d9, e2fa9d54), so presence of spec_hash cannot be the discriminator, and "at upgrade" in test 8 is not an event tp records anywhere. Two engineers write contradictory tests: one keys on a new per-round version stamp, one on a first-run marker written at upgrade, one on a config flag, one applies the reset to every round on disk (which §3 itself proves wrong: retroactively it moves blocking to round 8 and all to never). Test 5's nine-round replay is green only under the reading that the reset does not touch recorded rounds, which is exactly the reading left unpinned.
suggestion: Name the stored discriminator. tp already has the precedent: engine.IsLegacyRound (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:503-505) keys on the stored id_scheme marker and treats its absence as "recorded before that release". State the equivalent here -- e.g. ConsecutiveCleanSince stops only at a boundary between two rounds that both carry <marker> -- and restate test 8 as an assertion over that marker rather than over "at upgrade".

finding: §3's 'Prospective only' paragraph states the rule this release turns on -- 'The reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward' -- and names no mechanism by which an implementation can tell one kind of round from the other. A recorded round is engine.ReviewRound (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:17-42) and its whole surface is round, findings, clean, recorded_at, file, spec_hash, roles_hash, id_scheme, harness_note. None of those says which tp version recorded the round, and 'at upgrade' is not an event tp observes: there is no install timestamp to compare recorded_at against. So the hash-aware walk added by §3 traverses whatever is on disk and an old boundary cuts the streak exactly like a new one. That is not academic on this repository: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json's only two clean audit rounds are r8 (sha256:1259a4a) and r9 (sha256:54e031e) -- the hash moves between them -- so with audit_clean_rounds 2 the walk returns 1 and a converged, shipped cycle reports converged:false the moment the release is installed. §5 test 8 ('rounds already on disk at upgrade keep the consecutive_clean they had') is therefore an acceptance criterion I cannot satisfy from anything §3 states. tp already owns the pattern §3 needs and §3 does not cite it: ReviewRound.IDScheme exists for exactly this shape of problem ('empty on a legacy round recorded before this release'), with engine.IsLegacyRound as its reader.
suggestion: State the marker. Either (a) add a per-round field on the model of id_scheme -- e.g. `spec_hash_reset: true` stamped by --record from this release forward, with the walk treating a boundary as cutting only when the NEWER of the two adjacent rounds carries it, so a marker-less history can never cut; or (b) drop 'prospective' and state the reset as retroactive with spec/0.35.0.md as the named worked example and the operator's remedy; or (c) scope the reset to rounds after the newest marker-less round. Whichever is chosen, §5 test 8 needs the marker named, because 'the consecutive_clean they had' is a derived value with nothing stored to compare against.

finding: §3's two paragraphs specify mutually unimplementable behaviour, and the second one has no mechanism at all. 'Mechanism' says `consecutive_clean` 'is not stored: it is derived by `engine.ConsecutiveClean` walking `AuditRounds`', and the fix is `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince`, 'which stops the walk at the first `spec_hash` boundary, and the audit path calls it.' 'Prospective only' then says 'The reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward.' A pure function walking rounds on disk cannot honour that: every round already recorded carries a `spec_hash` (verified -- all nine of v0.35.0's audit rounds carry one, seven distinct values), and the walk stops at those boundaries the first time the upgraded binary runs. Nothing in a recorded round says which binary wrote it, and §3 forbids the two ways to know: the counter is derived rather than stored, so there is no pre-upgrade value to preserve, and no new stored field is proposed. §5 test 8 -- 'rounds already on disk at upgrade keep the `consecutive_clean` they had' -- is therefore unwritable against §3's mechanism, and it contradicts test 7, which requires a hash boundary between two clean rounds to leave `converged` false on rounds a fixture just wrote. The same gap falsifies test 5: replaying v0.35.0's nine recorded rounds through 'the audit path' gives `blocking` at 8 and `all` never (simulated: the only two clean-under-`all` rounds, r8 hash 1259a4af and r9 hash 54e031e6, are separated by a boundary), not the 3 and 9 test 5 asserts. This is the successor of round 3's `mechanism-falsifies-its-own-replay`, not a repeat of it: that finding asked for the retroactive clause to be dropped, the rewrite dropped the word and did not supply anything that makes prospectivity happen.
suggestion: Prospectivity needs a discriminator or it needs dropping. Either (a) store one -- a per-round marker written from this release forward, with the walk treating an unmarked round as boundary-free, which is a stored byte §3 currently rules out and should therefore say it is taking; or (b) drop 'prospective only', accept that the reset re-reads history, and re-measure §2.1's table and test 5 under the composed rule (the numbers are 8 and never, already simulated in §3); or (c) state that test 5's replay calls the un-reset predicate directly and is a §2-only assertion, and delete any claim that it reproduces what the shipped audit path reports. In all three cases §5 needs one test that composes §2 and §3, because the composition is where the release contradicts itself.

finding: Test 5 is the one test in §5 I cannot build, for two independent reasons, and it is the test that pins §2.1's whole argument. (1) Its fixture is this repository's live review state. I replayed both cycles and the numbers do reproduce -- spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 has 9 audit rounds, zero-`error` at r2 and r3 (blocking converges at 3) and zero non-PASS at r8 and r9 (all converges at 9); spec/.tp-review/0.36.0 has 13 rounds, zero-`error` at r2 and r3, and no round at zero non-PASS -- so the data exists. But spec/.tp-review/0.36.0 is the state directory of a cycle CLAUDE.md lists as **In flight**: recording one more audit round on spec/0.36.0.md changes 13 and can change 'never', and the assertion breaks with no defect. The gate wraps `go test -race ./...` in a before/after hash of spec/.tp-review/ precisely because the suite invokes tp against specs still in the repository; a test that reads 0.35.0's and 0.36.0's live round files makes the release's own acceptance a function of unrelated work. (2) The expected values are not determined by the inputs the test names. 'blocking at 3' and 'all at 9' are true only at audit_clean_rounds 2 (the value in .tp/config.json); at 1 blocking converges at round 2 and all at round 8. Neither §2.1's table nor test 5 states the parameter, and `engine.Converged` also folds `!StateStale(rounds, currentHash)`, so a replay must also be told what current hash to pass -- with eight distinct spec_hash values across v0.35.0's nine rounds, the answer moves.
suggestion: Freeze the fixture and state the parameters. Copy the row sequences into a testdata file committed with the release (severity and status per row is all the predicate reads -- roughly 130 rows for the two cycles), cite the commit the copy was taken at, and assert against the copy, not against spec/.tp-review/. Then state in test 5 the required_clean_rounds the replay runs at (2) and the current hash it passes (the last replayed round's own spec_hash), since both change the expected column. If replaying the live directories is intended, say so explicitly and say what happens when 0.36.0 records round 14.

finding: The release's only measurement is against its own feature and the comparison that would justify shipping it is never made. §2.1 concludes "`blocking` would have shipped over an `error` row in 2 of 2 measured cycles" and calls that decisive; §2 therefore defaults to `all`; §1 states "It does not change any existing project's behaviour". So the release adds surface for a value its only evidence says produced a worse outcome every time it was evaluated, reachable only by an operator who has read a spec file. Meanwhile this repository already ships the zero-surface answer to the same problem and has used it twice: CLAUDE.md's rule -- once spec-coverage is clean two rounds running and no round has produced a FAIL, record the out-of-surface findings with justification, name the version that takes them, and ship -- and spec/0.46.0.md §8 opens by recording that v0.36.0 shipped with `--status --check` at exit 1 "and shipping was still correct". §1 and §2 never say what `blocking` buys over that. The strongest candidate answer is a real one and the spec does not give it: the procedure needs a human, so it cannot end an audit phase under `tp run`, and `blocking` would make the stop machine-readable. If that is the case, it belongs in §1 -- and it makes the fence question critical rather than decorative, because a machine-readable stop any unit may set is not a stop.
suggestion: Add one paragraph to §1 naming the alternative and what the field buys over it. If the answer is unattended convergence, say so and let §2's `--skip-gate` sentence and the fence follow from it. If there is no answer beyond operator convenience, the honest release is smaller: §3's spec_hash reset is independently justified, costs no new field, and closes a real gap between the review and audit phases -- ship that and let spec/0.46.0.md §8 take the severity question with the role-scoping one it is already tied to.

finding: The rewrite replaced a correct measured constant with a wrong one, and the wrong one contradicts two later sections of the same file. §1 reads `Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus — 22 recorded rounds, 42 non-PASS rows`. The round-3 snapshot said `Across NINE recorded rounds the non-PASS rows were 3 error, 22 warning, 17 info`. Measured now: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/ holds audit-round-1..9.ndjson (9 files) and state.json carries 9 audit rounds; the non-PASS tally is 42 = 3 error + 22 warning + 17 info, so the row COUNT is 9 and 22 is the warning count copied into the wrong slot. §2.1's own table says `v0.35.0 | 9, converged` and §3 says `simulated against v0.35.0's nine rounds`, so the file now asserts 22 and 9 for the same quantity three sections apart. A decomposer sizing test 5's replay from §1 builds a 22-round fixture that cannot exist.
suggestion: Restore `nine recorded rounds`. Keep the 42/3/22/17 breakdown, which verifies exactly.

finding: §1 and §2.1 give opposite readings of the same measurement, and §1 never concedes the one the release actually acted on. §1: 'Two cycles in this repository and one field cycle in another project each ran long past the point where the only surviving findings were advisory' and '93% of what kept that phase open could not have blocked a release.' §2.1, on the same two repository cycles: 'v0.35.0's round 4 carries {error 1, warning 2, info 1} one round after `blocking` would have halted, and v0.36.0's rounds 7, 12 and 13 each carry `error` rows. **`blocking` would have shipped over an `error` row in 2 of 2 measured cycles.** That is decisive against it as a default.' Both are true of the corpus (verified: v0.35.0 r4 = error 1/warning 2/info 1; v0.36.0 r7 = 3 error, r12 = 2 error, r13 = 2 error) and they are true of different populations -- §1 counts ROWS over the whole phase, §2.1 counts what arrived AFTER the round `blocking` would have stopped at. The 93% therefore does not measure 'what kept that phase open': the rounds that kept v0.35.0 open past round 3 include round 4, whose error row is one of the three the 93% excludes. A reader of §1 alone concludes the loop wasted six rounds and that `blocking` is the right setting; a reader of §2.1 concludes the opposite and is the one the release followed. Nothing in §1 says the release's own measurement argues against the saving it advertises, and §1 never states the default.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §1 carrying §2.1's conclusion forward -- 'the same corpus also shows `blocking` stopping one round before an `error` row in both cycles, which is why the default stays `all` and the field is opt-in' -- and restate the 93% as what it counts: '93% of the non-`PASS` rows recorded in that phase were advisory.'

finding: §1 states the fixture size for the release's motivating measurement as "22 recorded rounds" and three other places state it as nine. Counted on disk: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 holds exactly 9 audit-round-N.ndjson files. Everything else in the sentence is exact -- 42 non-PASS rows, 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info, and 39/42 = 92.9% ~ 93% -- so the only wrong cell is the round count, and 22 is the warning figure from the same sentence duplicated into the round slot. §2.1 says "9, converged", §3 says "v0.35.0's nine rounds", and test 5 says "v0.35.0's nine recorded rounds". An engineer building test 5's fixture from §1 builds a 22-round fixture that does not exist.
suggestion: Change "22 recorded rounds" to "9 recorded rounds". The other four numbers in that sentence reproduce exactly and need no change.

finding: §1's headline measurement attributes two different corpora to one name in one sentence, and this round's rewrite introduced it: 'Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus -- 22 recorded rounds, 42 non-`PASS` rows: 3 `error`, 22 `warning`, 17 `info`.' Counted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/: v0.35.0's audit corpus is NINE rounds (audit-round-1..9.ndjson), and its non-PASS population is exactly 42 rows, 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info. The 22 is the round count of v0.35.0 AND v0.36.0 together (9 + 13), which is the same pairing §2 uses one paragraph later for the 2,913 PASS rows (1758 + 1155, verified correct). So one clause is scoped to both cycles and the next to one, under a single 'v0.35.0's own' attribution. Under the two-cycle reading the row figures are also wrong -- both cycles give 133 non-PASS rows, 18 error / 66 warning / 49 info, and 87.9% rather than 93%. It contradicts two later sections of its own file: §2.1's table row 'v0.35.0 | 9, converged' and §3's 'simulated against v0.35.0's nine rounds'. The pre-rewrite text at f9295e2 said 'Across nine recorded rounds', so this is a number the compression broke, not an inherited one.
suggestion: Write 'Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus -- nine recorded rounds, 42 non-`PASS` rows: 3 `error`, 22 `warning`, 17 `info`.' If the intent was the combined corpus, say 'across v0.35.0's nine and v0.36.0's thirteen audit rounds, 133 non-`PASS` rows: 18 `error`, 66 `warning`, 49 `info`' and re-derive the percentage, because 93% is a v0.35.0-only figure.

finding: §1's measurement sentence carries a round count that is false and that §2.1 contradicts two sections later. It reads 'Measured on v0.35.0's own audit corpus -- 22 recorded rounds, 42 non-`PASS` rows: 3 `error`, 22 `warning`, 17 `info`'. I recounted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json and its round files: that cycle has **9** audit rounds (and 21 review rounds -- neither is 22), and the other four figures are exactly right for those 9 rounds (42 non-PASS: error 3, warning 22, info 17). §2.1's own table then says 'v0.35.0 | 9, converged'. The likeliest provenance of the 22 is one of two slips, and both matter to a reader: it is the `warning` count repeated in the row above it, or it is 9 + 13, the audit rounds of v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 together -- in which case the sentence attributes a two-cycle round count to a one-cycle row population, since v0.36.0's audit rounds hold 91 non-PASS rows, not 42. This is the first number in the release and the one that sizes the problem; it is also the class CLAUDE.md names -- a quantifier over a set the author did not enumerate.
suggestion: Change '22 recorded rounds' to '9 recorded audit rounds' and check it against §2.1's first column, which is the artifact that already carries the number. If the two-cycle figure was intended, split the sentence: v0.35.0's 9 audit rounds hold 42 non-PASS rows (3/22/17), and say separately what v0.36.0's 13 hold.

finding: §1's scope sentence was rewritten in a way that both drops §3 from the release and asserts something §3 falsifies. It now reads `This release ships the field, its resolution, its validation and its documentation. It does not change any existing project's behaviour, because the default is the behaviour tp has today.` All four enumerated deliverables are §2; §3 (the spec-hash streak reset) appears in neither. And §3 IS a behaviour change that the default cannot neutralise: `all` only preserves which rows count, while §3 changes what `consecutive_clean` and `converged` report for any project whose spec moves mid-audit — which is why §3 needed a `Prospective only` paragraph at all. The round-3 snapshot's §1 covered both halves correctly (`the two things review already has: a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec`). My round-3 row `overview-undercounts-deliverables` said §1 undercounted at two of four; the repair reduced the enumeration to one section and added a false no-op claim on top.
suggestion: Enumerate what ships, one entry per section: `audit_converge_on with its resolution, validation and documentation, and a streak a changed spec ends`. Then qualify the no-op claim: the FIELD's default is today's behaviour; §3 changes reported convergence for a project whose spec moves, and that is intended.

finding: §2's predicate is stated over a 'surviving' set that this release explicitly declines to create, so the word means one thing in the section that defines the field and another in the Non-Goal that fences it. §2's table: '`all` | no non-`PASS` row survives'; '`blocking` | no surviving non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity'; then 'Both predicates are over non-`PASS` rows.' On the review side 'surviving' is a defined term -- engine/reviewclean.go's reviewFindingResolvedAway removes rows resolved wontfix/duplicate with evidence, and ReviewRoundClean counts only what is left -- and this section presents itself as that mechanism's twin. Non-Goal 2 says the audit side gets no such subtraction: '`--resolve` marks a row and convergence still counts it.' Verified in code: countAuditFindings (internal/cli/audit_record.go) increments on `!engine.AuditRowIsPass(row)` with no disposition check anywhere. So on the audit side 'surviving' is a synonym for 'recorded', and the release's central predicate is written in a vocabulary that says otherwise three times. It is not cosmetic: §5 tests 2, 3 and 4 each say 'a round with one surviving X row', and a test author cannot tell whether the fixture's row may carry a disposition -- under the review reading a disposed `error` row makes the round clean under `blocking`, under Non-Goal 2 it does not, and the guard §4 preserves asserts the latter.
suggestion: Drop the word. Write the table as 'no non-`PASS` row is recorded' / 'no recorded non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity', add one sentence -- 'on the audit side every recorded non-`PASS` row counts; there is no surviving-set subtraction, which is Non-Goal 2' -- and restate tests 2-4 as 'a round with one recorded X row'. If the subtraction IS intended, then Non-Goal 2 is wrong and the guard §4 preserves is being reversed a second time.

finding: §2.2 and test 4's justification are spent on rows the release never evaluates. `consecutive_clean` is derived by engine.ConsecutiveClean walking AuditRounds (§3's own words), and that walk reads a STORED boolean: ReviewRound carries `Findings int` and `Clean bool` stamped at record time (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:17-42), and ConsecutiveClean (reviewstate.go:429-438) breaks on `!rounds[i].Clean`. Nothing re-grades a recorded round's rows under a later audit_converge_on, and §3 makes the only new behaviour prospective. So the sixty-seven legacy rows sit in round files whose cleanliness is already decided; setting `blocking` cannot reach them. I counted the corpus rather than taking the number: 67 out-of-enum non-PASS rows (high 16, medium 15, low 36) across v0.29.0, v0.30.0, v0.31.0, v0.31.2 and v0.32.0 -- §2.2's figures reproduce exactly -- and 0 out-of-enum among the 238 non-PASS rows of v0.33.0-v0.36.0. That second number is what makes the framing costly rather than merely redundant: the live case is forward-looking (audit_schema.go:24 renders the enum into every prompt and, as §2 says, validates nothing, so an agent can emit `high` again) and §2.2 never states it, while test 4 tells the implementer the case "is not hypothetical" on the strength of a population the mechanism cannot see. A reader who believes that will not add the only test that matters -- a fresh round recording an out-of-enum severity.
suggestion: Keep the fail-closed rule; it is right. Replace §2.2's legacy-row argument with the forward claim in one sentence -- nothing validates `severity`, so an out-of-enum value can recur in a round recorded from here on, and it counts as blocking -- and keep the 67 rows only as the sentence that shows it has happened, not as the population the rule protects. In test 4, drop "so the case is not hypothetical": a fixture value's realism is not evidence about which rows the predicate reads. If §2.2's framing is meant literally, then the release owes the missing half -- what re-grades a recorded round -- and that is a much larger release than this one.

finding: `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince` is named but not signatured, and the one sentence describing it -- 'stops the walk at the first `spec_hash` boundary' -- admits two implementations that disagree on the case this release will meet most often. The existing walk is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds []ReviewRound) int` (engine/reviewstate.go:429). 'Since' implies a second argument, and the two candidates are: (a) `ConsecutiveCleanSince(rounds)`, walking back from the newest round and stopping when a round's spec_hash differs from the NEWEST ROUND's; or (b) `ConsecutiveCleanSince(rounds, currentHash)`, stopping at the first round whose hash differs from the LIVE SPEC's. They differ whenever the spec has been edited since the last recorded round -- the ordinary mid-loop state, and the state spec/0.37.0.md itself is in right now: (a) returns the trailing same-hash run, (b) returns 0. The choice also decides whether the new walk is redundant with `StateStale`, which `Converged` already ANDs in. §5 test 6 does not settle it: it gives the expected value for `ConsecutiveClean` (3, at hashes A, A, B) and gives none for `ConsecutiveCleanSince`, and both readings happen to return 1 on that one fixture, so the test as written cannot discriminate them.
suggestion: Write the signature and the return, e.g. `ConsecutiveCleanSince(rounds []ReviewRound) int` -- 'the length of the trailing run of clean rounds all sharing the newest recorded round's spec_hash' -- and say explicitly that the live spec hash is not an input, because StateStale already carries it. Then give test 6 the expected value for the new function (1 on the A, A, B fixture) and add a fixture where the two readings differ: rounds A, A clean with the live spec edited, where (a) returns 2 and (b) returns 0.

finding: §3 answers round 3's `mechanism-falsifies-its-own-replay` by asserting the opposite property, and the mechanism it states in the paragraph above cannot deliver it. Mechanism: `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince, which stops the walk at the first spec_hash boundary`. Property: `Prospective only. The reset applies to rounds recorded from this release forward.` A trailing walk over st.AuditRounds cannot tell a round recorded before the upgrade from one recorded after — nothing on engine.ReviewRound records a tp version, and §3 explicitly keeps the derived, zero-stored-bytes shape. Run against rounds already on disk the walk IS retroactive, which is why §3's own simulation gets 8/never on v0.35.0. The contradiction is load-bearing in §5: tests 6 and 7 require the walk to cut at a boundary, while test 5 (replaying v0.35.0's nine rounds to 3/9) and test 8 (`rounds already on disk at upgrade keep the consecutive_clean they had`) require it not to cut at the seven boundaries those same rounds carry. No stated rule discriminates them. Note also that the snapshot's §4 carried `The rounds themselves are not discarded — a recorded round stays a frozen fact` and old test 7 pinned it; both were deleted, and prospectivity is the one shape that plausibly needs to write something, so the guarantee was dropped in the round it started to matter.
suggestion: State the discriminator. Either the reset is derived and therefore retroactive, and §2.1's table plus test 5 are restated as `§2-only replays with the §3 walk disabled`; or a round records the marker that makes prospectivity computable (a recorded-under version, or a one-time upgrade watermark), in which case §3 stops being zero stored bytes and must restore the no-rewrite guarantee old test 7 held.

finding: §3 enumerates engine.Converged's consumers as "audit_record.go, run_status.go and budget.go" and that list is missing the one call site Non-Goal 4 exists to protect. Measured: engine.Converged is called from audit_record.go:95 and :333, run_status.go:149, budget.go:26 -- and review_status.go:67, which is REVIEW's --status (budget.go:26 also computes it for the review kind before overwriting at :28 with ReviewConverged). Non-Goal 4 promises "review's --status cannot move", but §3's list reads as though Converged were audit-only, and the release's own tests do not close the gap: test 6 guards engine.ConsecutiveClean, a different function. An implementation that folds ConsecutiveCleanSince into Converged in place -- rather than adding a variant -- leaves ConsecutiveClean untouched, passes test 6 unchanged, and silently moves review's --status converged. Round 3's finding on this covered the ConsecutiveClean half, which new test 6 now closes; the Converged half arrived with this round's §3 and is uncovered.
suggestion: Add review_status.go:67 to §3's list and say explicitly that it keeps calling the unchanged Converged. Add a test asserting review's --status converged and consecutive_clean are byte-identical before and after the change on a fixture whose review rounds straddle a spec_hash boundary -- the surface Non-Goal 4 names, rather than the function underneath it.

finding: §3 names one function it adds and requires a second it never names. 'it gains the same audit-side variant' is the whole specification of the audit-side `Converged`: no name, no signature, no call sites. §5 test 7 then makes that unnamed thing an acceptance criterion ('The audit-side `Converged` variant agrees with the reset'), so the task's acceptance cannot be written without me choosing the identifier -- and the identifier is the API this release ships. Two further gaps follow from the same sentence. §4 Non-Goal 4 says '§3 adds a function rather than altering the shared one' -- singular, where §3 requires two, so the countable claim in the Non-Goal does not describe the mechanism it is fencing. And §3's call-site list for the variant, 'reached by `audit_record.go`, `run_status.go` and `budget.go`', does not describe a swap at one of the three: `cli/budget.go:26` computes `engine.Converged(...)` unconditionally and then overrides it for review at :28, so the audit variant enters there as a change to an existing kind switch, not as a call replacement. (The same list also omits `cli/review_status.go:67`, which reaches the shared `Converged` from the review side -- harmless if the release only adds, but it makes the sentence false as a statement of who reaches the function.)
suggestion: Name it and give it a signature -- e.g. `AuditConverged(rounds []ReviewRound, requiredCleanRounds int, currentHash string) bool`, folding ConsecutiveCleanSince where Converged folds ConsecutiveClean -- and list the audit call sites that switch to it: audit_record.go:95, audit_record.go:333, run_status.go:149 and the non-review branch of budget.go:26. Fix Non-Goal 4 to say two functions, and state that engine.ConsecutiveClean and engine.Converged keep their present semantics for review.

finding: §3 states a closed-looking list of the audit callers that must gain the reset, and the list is short by exactly the caller the reset exists for. §3: `engine.Converged folds ConsecutiveClean internally and is reached by audit_record.go, run_status.go and budget.go; it gains the same audit-side variant`. Measured: engine.Converged is called on the audit side at internal/cli/audit_record.go:95 and :333, internal/cli/run_status.go:149, internal/cli/budget.go:26 — AND at internal/engine/resume.go:87, `auditConverged := Converged(auditRounds, wf.AuditCleanRounds, specHash)`, whose value feeds DetectPhase (engine/phase.go:33, the branch that returns `release`) and AuditConverged in engine/resumeblockers.go:40. So an implementation that satisfies §3 as written leaves `tp resume` reporting `phase: release` on a streak the reset has just invalidated. That is §3's own stated failure mode (`a reset that changes two printed integers while converged keeps the pre-reset answer is not a reset`) surviving in the one surface CLAUDE.md's reset-native workflow reads first. The list was inherited verbatim from round 3's implementer finding `chosen-form-misses-shared-predicate`, which enumerated the same four sites and also missed resume.go — so the omission entered the spec through a repair, not through the original draft.
suggestion: Name resume.go:87 in the list, or drop the enumeration and state the requirement instead: every audit-side caller of engine.Converged reads the hash-aware variant, with the test asserting `tp resume` on a boundary-split streak does not report phase `release`.

finding: §3's justification for "prospective only" rests on a count that is wrong: "simulated against v0.35.0's nine rounds, which carry eight distinct spec_hash values". Counted from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json, the nine audit rounds carry SEVEN distinct spec_hash values -- rounds 1 and 2 share 1acd1448 and rounds 7 and 8 share dc61f3d9; rounds 3,4,5,6,9 are distinct. This is the only quantitative claim in the paragraph that decides the release's most consequential design choice, and it is the one number a test replaying that corpus would falsify. The two conclusions drawn from it do reproduce under seven (retroactively, blocking's first pair of adjacent same-hash clean rounds is r7/r8 so it moves 3 -> 8; all's only clean rounds r8/r9 straddle a boundary so it moves 9 -> never), which is why the error is silent.
suggestion: Replace "eight distinct spec_hash values" with "seven distinct spec_hash values (rounds 1-2 and 7-8 each share one)", or bind the claim to the artifact instead of a literal -- "the spec_hash column of spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json" -- as CLAUDE.md's rule on quantifiers asks.

finding: Non-Goal 2 makes `a disposition that stops blocking` out of scope, and a downstream spec's entire stated dependency is that this release ships it. spec/0.41.0.md's header: `It ... depends instead on spec/0.37.0.md §3, which ships first: that release stops an accepted finding from blocking convergence, and this one gives it somewhere to live.` After 0f002ac both halves are false — §3 is now the spec-hash streak reset, and the premise is explicitly a Non-Goal — so 0.41.0 as written has no foundation and its `depends on 0.37.0` ordering is meaningless. Three more references broke in the same commit and CLAUDE.md's own rule requires the sweep after a renumber: CLAUDE.md:254 `0.41.0 is the durability half of 0.37.0 §3` (now points at the streak reset); CLAUDE.md:206-207 `spec/0.37.0.md §5 takes the divergence, so ... do not read --check as the ship signal until 0.37.0 lands` (§5 is now Tests, and Non-Goal 1 hands the divergence back to 0.46.0 §8, so 0.37.0 landing will not make --check readable); CLAUDE.md:132 `spec/0.37.0.md §5a takes it` (no §5a exists — it is spec/0.46.0.md §8a). CLAUDE.md:236's plan row still lists `accepted rows stop blocking` and `287` lines against a 149-line file whose second deliverable is now a Non-Goal.
suggestion: Run the cross-reference sweep CLAUDE.md mandates after a renumber: rewrite spec/0.41.0.md's header to depend on whichever release actually takes the disposition, and fix CLAUDE.md lines 132, 206-207, 236 and 254. A pointer that resolves to a file is not thereby correct.

finding: Three requirements were deleted from this release with a pointer to spec/0.46.0.md §8, and §8 holds only one of them. Measured: spec/0.46.0.md contains ZERO occurrences of `severity`, `wontfix`, `duplicate`, `disposition`, `--resolve` or `dedupAuditRows`; §8's entire subject is the role-scoping gap between `consecutive_clean` and the shipping rule. So Non-Goal 2 (`spec/0.46.0.md §8 records it` for the disposition-stops-blocking fork) and Non-Goal 3 plus §2's closing sentence (`Making that label checkable is spec/0.46.0.md §8's subject`) both point at text that does not exist. Only Non-Goal 1's `--check` pointer resolves, and it resolves because 4e26705 reverted 17d3007 exactly — no content was added to 0.46.0 by this cycle at all (`git show 4e26705 -- spec/0.46.0.md` is the byte-for-byte inverse of 17d3007's hunk). Commit 0f002ac's message claims all three `MOVED OUT to spec/0.46.0.md sec 8`; two of the three were deleted, not moved. This is the identical failure 4e26705's own message names — `the edit left the requirement in zero releases` — recurring in the same commit pair for two other requirements, and it costs more than a broken link: old §3 carried round 2's measurements (clean stamped at record time at audit_record.go:71 and :208; dedupAuditRows keeping the first (role,item_id) row and comparing nothing) and those now survive only as a compressed clause inside a Non-Goal that points somewhere they are not.
suggestion: Either add the two items to spec/0.46.0.md as §8c and §8d, carrying the measurements old §3 held, and keep 0.37.0's Non-Goals as pure pointers; or state in the Non-Goals that these are unowned and name the file that will take them. Do not leave a pointer that resolves to a file but not to a subject.

finding: §4 inventories the assertions of a protected guard it deliberately reverses, and the inventory is short by one -- the one that gives the guard its power. §4: 'the guard's other assertions -- that a `wontfix` disposition does not clear an open finding, and that `--check` stays shut over a disposed finding -- are untouched'; §5 test 9: '`TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate`'s two surviving assertions still pass.' Read at internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503, the test carries THREE surviving assertion groups after the `audit_converge_on` one is reversed: the wontfix one (:485-487), the `--check` one (:489-490), and a role_streaks entry-shape block (:492-502) whose core is `assert.Len(t, e, 3, "a streak entry carries role, consecutive_clean and open only")` plus a key-presence loop. That third one is not a detail. spec/0.33.0.tasks.json records why it was written -- 'a streak-entry shape assertion that would notice a per-role threshold or a scope label arriving' -- and spec/0.34.0.tasks.json's mutation sweep records that it is the assertion that kills a mutation of this guard: 'NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate = a fourth Threshold field added to engine.RoleStreak'. Neither of the two §4 names was the killing assertion. The omission composes badly with §3, which makes the top-level `consecutive_clean` reset at a `spec_hash` boundary while saying nothing about the per-role `consecutive_clean` inside role_streaks: if the reset is to be visible per role, the closed-set assertion §4 did not count is the thing that fails, and a unit reading §4 and test 9 would meet a red gate on a guard the spec told it was untouched. The test is also on spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md:56's protected list, which §4 does not mention.
suggestion: Say three, not two, and name the third: 'the role_streaks entry-shape assertion (`Len == 3`, role/consecutive_clean/open) is untouched, so this release adds no per-role field.' Make test 9 assert three. If §3's reset is meant to reach the per-role streak, that is a change to the guard and belongs in §4 as a second deliberate reversal with its own test; if it is not, say so in §3, because two counters named `consecutive_clean` in one payload with only one of them resetting needs stating. Either way name spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md:56 as the derivation that has to move with the reversal.

finding: Test 5 is the most expensive item in §5 and it buys a number, not a behaviour. It requires replaying v0.35.0's nine recorded audit rounds and v0.36.0's thirteen and reproducing four cells of §2.1. Two costs the release does not budget. (a) No shipped path produces that answer: per §3 the counter walks stored `Clean` flags (reviewstate.go:17-42, 429-438), so a counterfactual replay under a setting that was not in force needs a test-only harness that re-reads audit-round-*.ndjson and re-derives cleanliness under both values -- production code that exists only to reproduce a table in a spec. (b) The two corpora are live and one is in flight. spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/ holds audit-round-1..13 today and CLAUDE.md's release table marks v0.36.0 in flight; one more recorded audit round and test 5 fails for a reason that has nothing to do with audit_converge_on. The same directories already show why the boundary is not crisp: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/ carries snapshot-audit-round-10.md with no audit-round-10.ndjson, so even the "nine rounds" cell depends on whether the harness counts recorded rounds or snapshots. A test that a normal cycle in this repository can turn red is a round the loop pays for and learns nothing from.
suggestion: Split the claim from the fixture. Keep §2.1's numbers as a recorded one-off measurement, the way §1 already records "22 rounds, 42 non-PASS rows" without a test replaying it. Reduce test 5 to a frozen fixture -- either two small hand-written round sets that exercise the same shape, or the two corpora copied into testdata/ and named as a budgeted cost -- and state which. If the replay is kept against the live tree, say what happens when v0.36.0 records round 14, because someone will.

finding: Test 6 pins a number for the function that must NOT change and leaves the new function's answer unstated, so the assertion the release actually needs cannot be written. "engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince stops at a spec_hash boundary and engine.ConsecutiveClean does not. Three clean review rounds at hashes A, A, B still report consecutive_clean: 3." The `3` belongs to ConsecutiveClean; ConsecutiveCleanSince's expected return on that same fixture is never given, and both 1 and 2 are defensible because neither the round order nor the walk direction is stated (ConsecutiveClean, reviewstate.go:429-438, walks backwards from the end, so [A,A,B] yields 1 at the trailing boundary while [B,A,A] yields 2). Separately, "report consecutive_clean: 3" names no surface, and the two review surfaces do not share a function: review_status.go:91 emits it from engine.ConsecutiveClean (stored Clean flags) while review_record.go:204 emits it from engine.ReviewConsecutiveClean (reviewclean.go:119, recomputed live from the round's rows and severity-aware), so a fixture of three stored-clean rounds can produce 3 on one surface and a different number on the other.
suggestion: Give test 6 the full expected pair on one fixture -- e.g. rounds [A, A, B] in record order: ConsecutiveClean == 3 and ConsecutiveCleanSince == 1 -- and say which surface the `3` is read from (a direct engine call, or `tp review --status`, not `--record`).

finding: Test 7 as specified can pass against tp exactly as it ships today, so it does not discriminate the fixed implementation from the unfixed one. engine.Converged (internal/engine/reviewstate.go:509-511) is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash)`, and StateStale (:443-448) compares only the LAST recorded round's spec_hash against the current spec. Test 7 says "a hash boundary between the only two clean rounds leaves converged false, and --status --check exits 1 on the same input" without pinning where the current spec sits relative to those two rounds. The natural way to build that fixture -- record round 1, edit the spec, record round 2, and leave the tree as the test found it -- satisfies the assertion through the pre-existing !StateStale term whenever the spec was touched again after round 2, and both halves go green on unmodified code. Only a fixture in which the last round's spec_hash EQUALS the current spec hash isolates the §3 reset.
suggestion: Pin the fixture in test 7: two rounds, both clean, the boundary between round 1 and round 2, and the current spec byte-identical to what round 2 recorded (so StateStale is false and today's Converged returns true). Add the negative control the rule asks for -- the same fixture with no boundary must leave converged true -- so the test is observed failing before the reset exists.

finding: Test 9 -- "TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate's two surviving assertions still pass" -- states a count that is wrong, and §4 enumerates the same two. Counted in internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503: the reversal touches lines 473-474 (assert.NotEqual on the exit code, assert.Contains on "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on"); the surviving assertion sites are NINE -- :481, :484, :485, :490, :493, :494, :497, :498, :500 -- covering at least four distinct behaviours, not two. §4 names only two of them (the wontfix disposition at :485 and the --check exit 1 at :490) and never mentions the role_streaks entry-shape block at :493-502, which asserts each streak entry has exactly three keys (`assert.Len(t, e, 3, ...)`) and contains role, consecutive_clean and open. A unit implementing test 9 as "the two surviving assertions" has spec cover for deleting the shape block along with the reversed pair, and nothing would catch it.
suggestion: Either drop the count -- "every assertion in TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate other than the two on lines 473-474 still passes" -- or enumerate all four behaviours (--resolve succeeds, wontfix does not clear the open finding, --check stays shut, role_streaks entries keep their three-key shape). Binding the claim to line numbers rather than to a tally is what keeps it from rotting.

finding: Under `blocking` an agent cannot tell a genuinely clean round from a discounted one, and the release removes the requirement that it could without recording the decision. tp already solved this on the review side for the identical situation: spec/0.31.0.md §4.2 emits `nonblocking_open` -- the count of surviving non-blocking findings -- only on a clean round that has them, so presence itself signals accepted-open, and §8.4 keeps it through `--compact` as decision-critical. This release ships the same discount for audit and emits nothing, so `tp audit --record` returns `clean: true` and the agent must re-read the merged file to learn whether it discounted zero rows or twenty -- the round-trip `--record`'s summary exists to remove, and under `tp run` the only remaining reader after the authoring subagents exit. Round 3's §2.0a required an audit counterpart; the rewrite deleted the requirement rather than answering it, and I checked where it went: §4's five Non-Goals do not mention it and spec/0.46.0.md §8 is about `--check` role scoping, dispositions and making `severity` checkable. Nothing owns it. Note this is the inverse of my round-3 row, which said the counterpart was unbudgeted; dropping it was one of the two answers I named, but dropping it silently leaves the release emitting a `clean` an agent cannot interpret.
suggestion: One sentence in §2 either way. If the count ships, mirror §4.2 exactly -- emitted only on a clean round with surviving discounted rows, retained under `--compact`, one test -- and note that skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:634 and spec/0.31.0.md §8.4/test 18 currently state the field is review-only and never an audit field, so the docs and TestReviewNonBlockingOpen_AuditUnaffected move with it. If it does not ship, say so in §4 as a sixth Non-Goal with the reason, so the next cycle does not re-derive the question.

finding: §2 prices the whole release at one number and that number is an order of magnitude low. "engine/reviewconvergeon.go is twenty-four lines -- two constants, a hint string, and a predicate shared by the setter and every consumer -- and this is its twin." The file is indeed 24 lines. Counted across the tree, the identifier `review_converge_on` also appears in 14 production Go files (internal/cli: budget.go, config.go, config_extract.go, review.go, review_record.go, review_status.go, set.go, set_project.go, validate_project.go; internal/engine: projectconfig.go, reviewclean.go, reviewconvergeon.go; internal/model: projectconfig.go, workflow.go), 10 test files, and both shipped documents (skills/tp/SKILL.md, skills/tp/REFERENCE.md). That is what a workflow field costs in this codebase, and v0.31.1 exists because a previous field shipped without the config --extract and validate --project halves. The estimate matters because it is the only cost figure in a release whose §1 says nothing changes for anyone: an implementer reading "twenty-four lines" against §2.1's "six of nine rounds saved" gets a ratio the release does not have.
suggestion: Replace the twenty-four-line sentence with the footprint the twin actually requires -- resolution, the setter and its project form, config --extract, validate --project, budget, both docs -- or drop the number entirely and let §5 test 1 ("resolves through the full precedence chain") carry the scope. A count tied to an artifact survives; this one is tied to one file of the fourteen.

finding: §2 sizes this release against one artifact -- '`engine/reviewconvergeon.go` is twenty-four lines ... and this is its twin' -- and the file is indeed exactly 24 lines, but the twin is not a file, it is a field, and the field's measured surface is much larger than the sentence implies. Searching for review_converge_on / ReviewConvergeOn across the tree, the production (non-test, non-doc) files carrying it are fourteen: engine/reviewconvergeon.go, engine/reviewclean.go, engine/configresolve.go, engine/projectconfig.go, model/workflow.go, model/projectconfig.go, cli/set.go, cli/set_project.go, cli/config.go, cli/config_extract.go, cli/validate_project.go, cli/review.go, cli/review_status.go, cli/review_record.go, plus cli/budget.go and cli/import_enforce.go as consumers, and skills/tp/REFERENCE.md and SKILL.md as documentation §1 promises ('its documentation'). The precedent is this repository's own: v0.31.1 exists as a whole release because review_converge_on shipped in v0.31.0 without reaching `tp config --extract` and `validate --project`. §2 names 'the same precedence' and 'the same hint machinery' and nothing else, so those two surfaces -- the exact pair a prior release had to come back for -- are again the ones a decomposer must infer.
suggestion: Replace 'this is its twin' with the touch list, or point at it: 'audit_converge_on lands wherever review_converge_on lands -- model.Workflow and model.ProjectConfig, the resolver, the presence-preserving override marshalling, tp set --workflow (task and --project), tp config --extract, tp validate --project, and REFERENCE.md/SKILL.md'. Cite v0.31.1 as the reason the last two CLI surfaces are named rather than assumed. That turns §2 into three or four decomposable tasks instead of one 24-line one.

finding: The rewrite deleted the only cross-repository corroboration this release had, and §1's replacement sentence undercounts what the snapshot recorded. The snapshot carried TWO independent field cycles: §1's `A field cycle on a PHP package. Rounds 3 through 9 produced 15-30 findings each, zero FAIL in the last three, and never converged`, and §2.0a's `a Laravel package's 6-round Workflow D audit`, findings 15-3-1-2-1-1, spec-coverage 55/55 for four consecutive rounds, stopped by operator decision. §2.0a existed for a stated reason — `a single repository's numbers are a weak argument for a default` — and the new §1 reads `Two cycles in this repository and one field cycle in another project`, so a second measured cycle became one. The default is now decided in §2.1 from this repository's two cycles alone, and the snapshot's own hedge on that sample (`one sample each way is not a policy`) was replaced by `That is decisive against it as a default`. The Laravel measurement itself is not lost — spec/0.46.0.md §8a still cites that cycle's rounds 4-6 — but 0.37.0 no longer counts it and no longer states the sample-size caveat it was recorded to answer.
suggestion: Restore the count (`two field cycles in two other projects`) and one line of §2.0a's numbers, or soften `decisive` back to what N=2 supports: `2 of 2 measured cycles, which is why the conservative value is the default and the field is opt-in`.

finding: §3 enumerates the call sites of one function and not the other, and the unenumerated ones are the audit path's own. It says `ConsecutiveClean` 'is shared with review's `--status`, so this release **adds** `engine.ConsecutiveCleanSince` ... and the audit path calls it', then enumerates only `Converged`'s reach ('`audit_record.go`, `run_status.go` and `budget.go`'). Measured across internal/ (non-test): `engine.ConsecutiveClean` has four callers -- cli/audit.go:352, cli/audit_record.go:101, cli/audit_record.go:339 and cli/review_status.go:91. Three of the four are the audit path, and each one is a printed `consecutive_clean` integer that must switch to the new function; §3 names none of them while its own rationale ('a reset that changes two printed integers while `converged` keeps the pre-reset answer is not a reset') turns on there being printed integers. The `Converged` list is right for the audit reach -- I checked budget.go:21-33, whose review branch already calls ReviewConverged and whose audit branch keeps Converged, so the split §3 proposes already exists there in the review direction -- which makes the missing half more visible, not less: the release specifies a new function for a phase-scoped predicate and leaves it to a decomposer to find the three sites that must call it, in the same release whose §1 hazard is a counter that keeps a pre-reset answer.
suggestion: Enumerate both, as §3 already does for `Converged`: '`ConsecutiveClean` is reached on the audit path by `audit.go`, `audit_record.go` (twice) and, for review, `review_status.go`; the three audit sites call `ConsecutiveCleanSince` and `review_status.go` does not.' That is also the acceptance a task can be written against, and it makes Non-Goal 4's 'review's `--status` cannot move' checkable rather than asserted. Consider instead the shape budget.go already uses -- one function with a phase parameter -- so a future audit-side predicate does not need a third twin.

finding: §4's guard-reversal paragraph and §5 test 9 both count the surviving assertions of `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` and both undercount, and the paragraph also leaves the reversal itself underdetermined. I read the test (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503). Its assertion groups are four, not three: (i) 472-474, two assertions -- `assert.NotEqual(code, 0)` plus `assert.Contains(..., "unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on")` -- the pair the release reverses; (ii) 483-487, wontfix does not clear go-safety's open finding; (iii) 489-490, `--status --check` still exits 1 over the disposed finding; (iv) 492-502, a loop asserting every role_streaks entry carries exactly three keys. §4 names (ii) and (iii) as 'the guard's other assertions' and test 9 pins 'the two surviving assertions'; (iv) survives too and is unmentioned, so a task whose acceptance is 'the two surviving assertions still pass' does not cover the test. Separately, 'Shipping the field reverses that assertion' does not say which of two edits to make: delete the block, or invert it to assert that `set --workflow --project audit_converge_on=blocking` now exits 0. They are different tasks and only the second leaves a guard behind; the test's name and its doc comment at 365-369 ('that test also pins Non-Goals 2 and 5') describe the file after either edit differently.
suggestion: Say 'its three surviving assertion groups', or drop the count and name them ('the wontfix, the --check exit code and the role_streaks entry shape'). State which edit the reversal is: 'the two assertions at 472-474 are replaced by their inverse -- the set succeeds and audit_converge_on resolves to blocking' is the form that keeps a guard, and it makes test 9 a positive assertion rather than a survival count.

finding: Test 4 names three inputs and then pins a fixture that can supply only one of them: "a row whose severity is absent, null, or outside the enum is counted as blocking. The fixture uses one of the 67 recorded legacy rows, so the case is not hypothetical." Counted across spec/.tp-review/0.29.0-0.32.0, the 67 out-of-enum rows carry high 16, medium 15, low 36 and nothing else -- every one has a present, non-null string severity -- so the legacy fixture exercises "outside the enum" and neither of the other two. "Absent" and "null" also need a stated relationship: whether they are two cases or one depends on how a row is decoded (a map[string]any keeps them apart, a struct string field collapses both to ""), and §2's fail-closed rule reads on "unrecognised severity" without saying which of the two it covers.
suggestion: Split test 4 into three assertions with three fixtures: a synthetic row with no severity key, a synthetic row with severity: null, and one recorded legacy row (any of the 67 high/medium/low). Keep the legacy row as the third case only -- it is the one that is not hypothetical.

finding: Test 4 pins its own fixture to recorded data -- 'The fixture uses one of the 67 recorded legacy rows, so the case is not hypothetical' -- and names neither the row nor the file it comes from, nor whether 'uses' means read from spec/.tp-review/ at test time or copy the row's text into the test. I verified §2.2's population is exactly right (67 out-of-enum non-PASS rows across v0.29.0-v0.32.0: high 16, medium 15, low 36, in 15 round files), so a row exists to pick; but the three cases test 4 lists -- severity absent, `null`, outside the enum -- are not all covered by that population: every one of the 67 carries a string severity, so the absent-key and JSON-null cases have no recorded instance and must be synthesised anyway. Left as written the task either reads the repository's live state directory (the same hazard as test 5) or invents the fixture, and only one of those is what the sentence claims.
suggestion: Name the row and the mode: e.g. 'the fixture inlines one recorded legacy row verbatim (spec/.tp-review/0.32.0/audit-round-N.ndjson, severity `high`) alongside two synthesised rows for the absent and `null` cases, which the 67 do not exhibit.' A copied literal keeps the not-hypothetical claim and does not couple the release's tests to a mutable directory.

finding: Test 5 kept the hard-coded expectations of the old test 4 and dropped the sentence that argued they were runnable at all. Old test 4 closed: `The replay reads status and severity off recorded rows and needs no spec snapshot, which is why it is runnable where spec/0.43.0.md §6's corpus gates are not.` That is a correct and load-bearing citation — CLAUDE.md records that a gate phrased as `replay the recorded rounds` cannot run, because 35 of 156 recorded review rounds carry a snapshot whose sha256 is not the spec_hash the round recorded, and this replay escapes that because it never reads a snapshot. New test 5 keeps `blocking at 3, all at 9` and `blocking at 3 and all never` against spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 and /0.36.0 — live, committed, mutable repository state that nothing pins — with the reason it is safe deleted. I re-verified the numbers hold today (0.35.0 r2 {info 7, warning 5} and r3 {info 3, warning 2} carry zero error, r8 and r9 are the only fully-PASS rounds; 0.36.0 r2 and r3 carry zero error and no round reaches zero non-PASS), so the test is correct now and unprotected against any later `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md --record` in this repository.
suggestion: Restore the runnability sentence and add what it implies: the replay copies the round files into the test's own tempdir fixture, so a later recorded round against those specs cannot move the expectation.

finding: The old test list pinned this release's most contested decision and the new one does not. Old test 1: `audit_converge_on resolves through the documented precedence WITH DEFAULT blocking`. New test 1: `audit_converge_on resolves through the full precedence chain, and an invalid value is refused with the same hint shape review_converge_on uses` — the default value is gone from the assertion. The default flipped from `blocking` to `all` this round and is the single decision §2.1 spends a whole subsection defending; §1's `It does not change any existing project's behaviour` is true only if the built-in default is `all`. Nothing in §5 would fail if an implementation shipped `blocking` as the built-in. That is a dropped assertion whose subject not only stayed in scope but became the release's headline decision.
suggestion: Restore the default to test 1: `resolves through the full precedence chain with built-in default all`, and add the corollary the no-op claim rests on — a project with no audit_converge_on set records the same clean/converged verdicts as the previous release.

finding: The one behaviour that produces the measured saving has no test. Under `blocking` the field's entire value comes from discounting `warning` rows: §1's "93% advisory" is 22 warning and 17 info of 42 on v0.35.0, and counted across every audit corpus in the tree, `warning` is 158 of the 360 non-PASS rows -- the largest class by a wide margin. §5 tests `info` (test 2), `error` (test 3) and an out-of-enum value (test 4), and never `warning`. So the enum's middle value, the one carrying the saving, is pinned by nothing: an implementation that graded `warning` as blocking would pass all nine tests and reduce `blocking` to a slower `all`, reproducing the exact stall the release exists to end -- and it would not be caught by the §2.1 replay either, because test 5's cells come from the same rounds only if the predicate is already right. This is CLAUDE.md's own boundary rule: a behavioural test can verify a rule and still miss its boundary.
suggestion: Extend test 2 to name both non-blocking values rather than adding a test: "Under `all`, a round with one surviving `info` row and a round with one surviving `warning` row are not clean; under `blocking`, both are." That is one clause, it pins the full enum against test 3's `error` and test 4's unknown, and it makes §1's 93% figure an assertion rather than a measurement.

finding: The v0.36.0 half of test 5 -- new this round -- pins expected values to a cycle that is still running, in a directory whose file layout will double-count if replayed by glob. CLAUDE.md lists v0.36.0 as "In flight"; spec/.tp-review/0.36.0 today holds audit-round-1..13.ndjson, and a fourteenth round recorded during this release's own implementation changes both pinned answers ("blocking at 3" survives, since it is decided by rounds 1-3, but "all never" is falsified the moment any later round records zero non-PASS rows). The same directory also holds per-role files audit-r9-spec-coverage.ndjson through audit-r13-maintainability-conventions.ndjson beside the merged rounds, so a replay harness globbing audit-*.ndjson reads rounds 9-13 twice; spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 has no per-role files, so a harness written against the v0.35.0 half alone will not surface this.
suggestion: Freeze both corpora as fixtures -- copy the audit-round-N.ndjson files and state.json into testdata/ at the counts the table asserts -- and say the replay reads audit-round-N.ndjson by round number, not by directory glob. That also keeps the test off the live spec/.tp-review/ tree that scripts/check-suite-state.sh hashes.

finding: §2's population clause -- "Both predicates are over non-PASS rows" -- is normative, is the reason the spec gives for not phrasing the predicate over "any row of any severity", and no test in §5 exercises it. Tests 2, 3 and 4 all construct non-PASS rows, so all three pass identically under a predicate scoped to non-PASS rows and under one scoped to every row. The case that separates them is a PASS row carrying a blocking severity, and it cannot be drawn from the corpus: measured across v0.35.0's and v0.36.0's audit rounds, all 2,913 PASS rows carry severity null (the spec's own figure, reproduced exactly). That makes the clause true today by the emitters' habit rather than by anything tp enforces -- §2 says in the next paragraph that severity is self-declared and unvalidated, so a future auditor emitting {status: PASS, severity: error} is not prevented.
suggestion: Add a test: under blocking, a round whose only severity-error row has status PASS is clean; under all, the same round is clean. It is the assertion that distinguishes the shipped predicate from the one §2 explicitly rejects, and it costs one synthetic row.

finding: Near-miss, caught before recording. Seeing "22 recorded rounds" beside "22 warning" in the same sentence, I formed the conclusion that §1's whole measurement was transcribed from somewhere else and unreproducible, and was about to file it as a critical over the release's motivating figure. finding: Near-miss, reported per the round's instruction. The rewrite deleted the snapshot §2.1 paragraph carrying a measured defect in shipped code — `engine.WriteSnapshotAtomic builds its temporary file from a fixed final + .tmp, so role units that REFERENCE.md runs parallel with their siblings collide and the loser's rename fails with ENOENT — measured on the literal brief commands at 0/20 sequential and 5/40 parallel`. finding: Nothing in the release states an exit code for any path. §2's only error-path sentence is 'rejected with the same hint machinery when the value is neither', and §5 test 1 says 'refused with the same hint shape review_converge_on uses'. The twin distinguishes two codes that the phrase 'the same hint machinery' collapses: engine/reviewconvergeon.go's own doc comment says the set commands surface the hint on a rejected literal argument at exit 2, while a consuming command surfaces it when a stored winning value fails to resolve at exit 1. An implementer following the twin will get this right; an implementer following §2 has to go read the twin to find out there are two, and test 1 as written passes whichever single code is chosen.
suggestion: Add the codes to test 1: 'tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=<bad> exits 2 with `must be one of: all, blocking`; a consuming command over a stored bad value exits 1 with the same hint.' Also state the hint string's word order, since it is a literal a test will assert on.

finding: Near-miss, self-caught. The wrong conclusion I was about to write: '§2.2 creates an unconvergeable state -- under `blocking` the fail-closed rule makes all 67 legacy rows blocking, 51 of which (`medium` 15, `low` 36) are severities tp itself classifies as explicitly NON-blocking on the review side (engine/reviewclean.go's nonBlockingReviewSeverities), and §2.2 offers no migration, Non-Goal 2 forbids a disposition from clearing them and Non-Goal 3 forbids checking them -- so a project carrying legacy rows in its trailing rounds can set `blocking` and never converge.' It is false, and the reason is a one-line lattice check I nearly skipped: `blocking`'s clean set is a superset of `all`'s, because both predicates are over the same non-`PASS` population and `blocking` only removes rows from it. A legacy row that blocks under `blocking` already made its round unclean under today's behaviour, so the fail-closed rule can never make a round dirtier than the status quo and cannot create a dead end that did not already exist. §2.2's 'the conservative answer and needs no migration' is sound as written, and all its numbers check out against the corpus (67 out-of-enum non-`PASS` rows, high 16 / medium 15 / low 36, in exactly fifteen round files across 0.29.0, 0.30.0, 0.31.0, 0.31.2 and 0.32.0). Recording it because the shape is general and this cycle keeps meeting it: a section that repairs a false claim reads as false, and what separated the two here was checking the direction of the change rather than its magnitude.
suggestion: No spec change. §2.2 is the most defensible section in the file. If anything is added, one clause making the monotonicity explicit -- '`blocking` never counts a round dirtier than `all` does, so no setting of this field can make a previously clean round unclean' -- would retire this reading for the next reader and is a testable statement.

finding: Three conclusions I formed this round and dropped before recording. (1) I had drafted that §3's call-site list ('reached by audit_record.go, run_status.go and budget.go') omits cli/audit.go:352, where engine.ConsecutiveClean feeds the auditor prompt's streak framing, and engine/resume.go, where the oracle's auditConverged is computed -- so the prompt and tp resume would keep the pre-reset answer. Checking review-round-2.ndjson first: round 2's `reset-of-a-derived-value` already enumerates audit.go:352 and resume.go:87 and is still unresolved, so this is the same finding at a new line number, not a new one. What survived the check is only the part that is a property of the citation list as now written -- budget.go being a kind switch rather than a call site -- which I folded into the unnamed-variant row. (2) I had drafted that §2's `blocking` predicate is undefined because 'surviving' is never defined for audit rows, since audit `clean` is stored at record time while review's is recomputed live (review_status.go:63-65). Round 1/2 already carry '§2 never says whether audit_converge_on is evaluated LIVE against each recorded round', unresolved, so this is that finding. (3) I had drafted that §2's severity claims are false, on the strength of round 1's still-unresolved critical that '§2's safety argument rests on a false code claim' about severity being validated. The rewrite inverted the claim rather than repeating it, so I checked the new text instead of inheriting the old verdict: `severity` appears zero times in cli/audit_record.go, and among production files only cli/audit_schema.go carries it on the audit path -- so 'validates nothing', 'validates category alone' and 'nothing on the audit path reads severity at all' are all true as now written. §2's 2,913-PASS-rows-at-severity-null claim is also exact (I counted 2,913, every one with the key present and JSON null). No finding.
suggestion: No action beyond the rows recorded. The habit worth keeping: when a whole-file rewrite inverts a claim a previous round falsified, re-measure the new claim rather than carrying the old verdict forward -- here the inversion was correct and re-reporting it would have been the round's worst row.

finding: Second near-miss. Old test 6 read `resets consecutive_clean to zero AND reports the reset on the machine-readable surface`, and the new §5 has no equivalent of the second clause. Comparing the two test lists mechanically, I had this queued as a dropped assertion whose subject is still in scope — under tp run the orchestrator branches on machine-readable output, so an unreported reset looked invisible. It is a correct deletion: round 3's ax-economist filed `withdrawn-mechanism-left-its-output-key` against exactly that clause, measuring that audit --status already emits audit_rounds in full (internal/cli/audit_record.go:337-344) with every entry's spec_hash beside consecutive_clean, so a dedicated reset key would be a field on every payload restating two fields the reader already parses. The wrong conclusion would have been to demand the key back, re-opening a finding the rewrite closed correctly. The half of that comparison that DOES survive — old test 7's no-rewrite guarantee — is filed above under §3, because prospectivity is what puts writing back on the table.
